If you're on the fence about installing macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple's long list of security fixes might be enough to convince you. And if you're sticking with an older version, it's best to install macOS Tahoe 26.7 or macOS Sequoia 15.7 as soon as possible. Here's why.

Apple fixes 200+ macOS vulnerabilities

Apple today published the full security release notes for macOS 27 Golden Gate, macOS Tahoe 26.7, and macOS Sequoia 15.8, detailing more than 200 vulnerabilities addressed in this round of updates.

As with several recent macOS updates, Apple's acknowledgements include a number of AI-focused security teams and researchers, including OpenAI Codex Security, NVIDIA AI Red Team, and Anthropic Research.

The fixes included in macOS 27 cover a wide range of flaws that could allow malicious apps or attackers to execute arbitrary code with kernel or root privileges, escape the macOS sandbox, bypass Gatekeeper protections, modify protected system files, access sensitive user data, and more.

For example, an AVEVideoEncoder vulnerability could allow a sandboxed app to execute arbitrary code with kernel privileges. Meanwhile, a UDF file system vulnerability could likewise allow apps to execute code at the kernel level. Apple also addressed flaws that could lead to remote code execution via Bluetooth, CUPS, and WebDAV.

As for macOS Tahoe 26.7 and macOS Sequoia 15.8, both updates patch many of the same vulnerabilities noted above, including several kernel-level, root privilege, sandbox escape, Gatekeeper bypass, and remote code execution flaws.

Older versions of the system also have some additional fixes not listed in macOS 27, including an ImageIO vulnerability in macOS Sequoia 15.8 that could lead to arbitrary code execution when processing a specially crafted malicious image.

  • About the security content of macOS Tahoe 26.7
  • About the security content of macOS Sequoia 15.8

Will you be upgrading to macOS 27 Golden Gate, or sticking with macOS Tahoe 26? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
